Testimony in Support of Comprehensive Resources for Veterans Introduction Chairperson and esteemed members of the committee, Thank you for the opportunity to address this body on behalf of the brave men and women who have selflessly served our nation. Today, I am here to express strong support for several critical initiatives aimed at providing meaningful resources to veterans and their families. These proposals—from supporting veteran vendors to prioritizing affordable housing access— are not merely policies; they are a reflection of our collective gratitude and responsibility to honor those who have served. Supporting Veteran Vendors: Removing Barriers to Entrepreneurship Veterans have demonstrated exceptional leadership, discipline, and resilience in their military service. Many leverage these qualities to become entrepreneurs, contributing to local economies and fostering innovation. However, they often face significant financial and logistical barriers. By waiving permit fees for mobile food unit commissaries that reserve space for veteran vendors, we can help level the playing field. This initiative reduces financial strain, enabling veterans to establish sustainable businesses, create jobs, and participate more fully in our local economies. Supporting veteran vendors is not just good policy; it is a tangible way to empower those who have given so much to our nation. Cure Periods for Veterans Service Organizations: Preserving Mission-Critical Services Veterans Service Organizations (VSOs) are the backbone of community-based support for veterans. These organizations provide essential services, including counseling, job placement assistance, and advocacy. However, they often operate with limited resources and face regulatory challenges that can hinder their effectiveness. Establishing cure periods for certain violations would grant VSOs the opportunity to address compliance issues without incurring immediate penalties. This approach ensures that these organizations can continue their critical work uninterrupted while maintaining accountability. It is a balanced and compassionate solution that reflects our commitment to supporting organizations dedicated to serving veterans. Rental Assistance for Homeless Veterans: A Lifeline for Stability The issue of veteran homelessness is a moral and societal crisis. Many veterans face unique challenges, including post-traumatic stress disorder, physical disabilities, and economic hardship, which increase their risk of homelessness. Rental assistance programs specifically tailored to veterans are a proven strategy for addressing this urgent issue.

Haspel-Staab Post 55161-55 69th Street Middle Village, NY 11379 Expanding rental assistance ensures that homeless veterans have access to stable housing, a foundational step in their journey toward reintegration and self-sufficiency. By prioritizing this initiative, we affirm our commitment to ensuring that no veteran is le ft without a roof over their head. Property Tax Exemption for Veterans with 100% Service-Connected Disabilities (S.2028- A/A.2965-A) V eterans who have sustained 100% service-connected disabilities have made profound sacrifices in defense of our nation. These individuals face significant physical and financial challenges that make homeownership and economic stability particularly difficult. The proposed property tax exemption under S.2028-A/A.2965-A is a critical step in alle viating these burdens. By reducing the financial strain of property taxes, we can help disabled veterans maintain homeownership and stability, ensuring they receive the recognition and support they deserve. This measure is not just financial relief; it is an acknowledgment of their extraordinary service and sacrifice. Public Housing Admission Preferences for Veterans Affordable housing is increasingly out of reach for many, especially in urban areas like New York City. Veterans, who have given so much to our country, deserve prioritized access to public housing to help them reintegrate into civilian life with dignity and sta bility. Including an admission preference for veterans in the New York City Housing Authority’s (NYCHA) next proposed agency plan would ensure that veterans have a fair opportunity to secure affordable housing. This policy not only addresses a pressing need but also demonstrates our unwavering commitment to those who have served. Conclusion: A Call to Action These initiatives represent more than policy proposals; they embody our nation’s commitment to honor and support its veterans. By waiving permit fees for veteran vendors, granting cure periods for VSOs, expanding rental assistance, enacting property tax exemptions, and prioritizing public housing access, we take meaningful steps to improve the lives of those who have sacrificed so much for us. I urge this committee to act decisively in advancing these measures. Let us reaffirm our sha red obligation to those who have served and ensure they have the resources, support, and opportunities they so richly deserve. Thank you for your time and consideration. Respectfully submitted, Sean C. Baltrusitis Commander, Haspel-Staab VFW Post 551 (C) 917/834-3363 E-Mail: seanbvfw551@outlook.com

WILLIAMS TO THE NEW YORK CITY COUNCIL COMMITTEE ON FIRE AND EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT JANUARY 29, 2025 Good Morning, My name is Jumaane D. Williams, the Public Advocate for the City of New York. Thank you to Chair Ariola and committee members for holding today's hearing. As climate change continues to impact our city in unpredictable ways, we have a responsibility to be informed, prepared, and protected from dangerous weather. As we saw in 2024, this weather is not confined to one specific challenge. In April, a 4.8 magnitude earthquake shook the city. 1 In August, a flash flood caused widespread flooding across the city, resulting in residents in need of rescue, abandoned vehicles, and power outages. 2 3 Two months later, the lack of expected rainfall resulted in the driest October in the city’s recorded history, forcing New Yorkers to conserve daily water usage. 4 This drought also caused wildfires in and around the city, endangering residents and impacting our air quality with orange and polluted skies. 5 We know that these fires, which are magnified by drought conditions, are usually the result of accidental ignition. At the end of last year, I published a report on the danger of fires caused by lithium-ion batteries and will continue to call for safety measures that prevent these dangerous blazes. Altogether, these occurrences are not an anomaly but a growing issue that demands our attention and preparedness. Flash floods present the most frequent and dangerous of these natural occurrences, greatly impacting communities with lower elevation levels in Southeastern Queens, South Brooklyn, and the Bronx. 6 These high risk areas are compounded by basement units which may not be properly secured against heavy rainfall. According to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, there are more than 4,000 below ground units that are at risk of major flooding, events which are not only dangerous and costly but potentially life threatening. 7 New solutions must also include neighborhoods that may not be coastal but are disproportionately impacted by flash flooding. Interior sections of Brooklyn and Queens, like Hollis, Queens, are in need of a thorough reassessment due to groundwater levels and predevelopment conditions.
